The Naked Schizothoracin (Oxygymnocypris stewartii) is a large cyprinid endemic to the Yarlung Tsangpo River system on the Tibetan Plateau, where it occupies cold, high-altitude waters. Field surveys indicate that males standard length at puberty occurs at 27.3 centimeters [Lp = 27.3 centimeters], a size considerably smaller than the female standard length at puberty which has been measured at 35.7 centimeters [Lp = 35.7 centimeters], suggesting a pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation size. This species is known to reach a maximum standard length approaching 59 centimeters [Li = 59 centimeters], a value that ranks it among the larger native ichthyofauna of the region. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analyses reveal that the ultimate body size is attained following a prolonged period of somatic investment, reflecting the constraints imposed by the cold, oligotrophic environment of its native habitat. The protracted growth phase is not unique among plateau schizothoracines, but O. stewartii appears to achieve a larger terminal size than many of its sympatric congeners, a trait likely linked to its piscivorous feeding ecology and position as an apex predator within this simplified fish community.

Reproductive life-history parameters for this species have been characterized from both field collections and laboratory holding studies. Eggs are demersal and measure approximately 2.32 mm in diameter, from which the wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.0065 grams [Wwb = 0.0065 grams], reflecting the small, volky ova typical of broadcast-spawning cyprinids. This minute birth mass, though derived from an egg volume calculation, is consistent with the minute, nutrient-poor oocytes produced in large numbers by many cyprinids, an adaptation that trades individual offspring provisioning for high fecundity. Following fertilization, the yolk-sac larva emerges from the egg and enters a lecithotrophic stage, during which endogenous reserves are progressively depleted until the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk absorption stage is relatively extended in this species, likely a consequence of the low metabolic rates sustained at the prevailing water temperatures. In contrast to many lowland cyprinids, the larval period of O. stewartii appears to be characterized by slow, steady development, with the exotrophic transition occurring only after a substantial portion of the yolk reserve has been assimilated. Observations of captive-reared individuals indicate that the first feeding larvae actively pursue zooplankton once the mouth gapes sufficiently, marking the end of the obligate dependence on maternally derived resources.

Marking its position as one of the largest plateau cyprinids, adult individuals of this species achieve an ultimate wet weight of 2,530 grams [Wwi = 2,530 grams], reflecting the considerable somatic investment required to sustain an apex predator role in an oligotrophic cold-water system. This asymptote in body mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth over early reproduction, a pattern observed in many high-elevation fishes that experience brief growing seasons and low annual productivity. The large terminal body size likely confers advantages in terms of gape-limited predation and intraspecific competition for spawning territories. Comparative data from other plateau-dwelling schizothoracins suggest that O. stewartii occupies the upper end of the body-size spectrum within this clade. The attainment of such a substantial adult mass implies a long period of somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive maturity, a trajectory that is reflected in the relatively late ages at puberty recorded for both sexes in this species.

Life-history studies conducted at a water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C] have provided key demographic data for this species. Under these thermal conditions, the maximum lifespan has been estimated at approximately 9,125 days [am = approximately 9,125 days], a value that translates to roughly 25 years and ranks among the greatest longevities documented for any Tibetan Plateau cyprinid at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This extreme longevity is consistent with predictions from metabolic theory for a large-bodied, cold-water ectotherm with a slow pace of life. Such an extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive events over the life cycle, although the frequency of spawning events is likely constrained by the short annual window of favorable thermal and hydrological conditions in the high-altitude rivers. This combination of large final size and extreme longevity, rare even among other long-lived schizothoracines, positions O. stewartii as an outlier in life-history space within the subfamily Schizothoracinae. The population dynamics of O. stewartii are likely sensitive to any increase in adult mortality, as the species invests heavily in reaching a large size and old age.

Detailed age-at-maturity estimates, also derived from rearing experiments and otolith readings conducted at the same 9 °C [T = 9 °C] thermal regime, reveal significant differences between the sexes. Females attain puberty at approximately 2,665 days since birth [tp = approximately 2,665 days since birth], a value that corresponds to around 7.3 years, while males reach this developmental milestone considerably earlier, at about 1,862 days since birth [tp = about 1,862 days since birth], equivalent at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C] at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]to roughly 5.1 years. This pronounced sexual bimaturism, with females delaying puberty by over two years relative to males, is a classic pattern in polygynous or size-dimorphic species where female reproductive success is strongly correlated with body size. The delay allows females additional time for somatic growth before the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis, thereby maximizing their fecundity at first spawning. Males, by contrast, may benefit from earlier maturation to establish territories and secure breeding opportunities, even at a smaller adult size. The high degree of sexual dimorphism in both age and size at puberty in O. stewartii highlights the contrasting selective pressures operating on the two sexes in this extreme environment.
